evidence: src/application/project-service.ts: ProjectService(projects: ProjectRepository, ids: IdGenerator, clock: Clock) uses Project.create and projects.save, and getProject throws NotFoundError("Project", id)
src/application/task-service.ts: TaskService uses Task.create, tasks.save, task.assignTo and task.markDone, so domain behaviour is delegated to the entity
src/application/user-service.ts: UserService(users: UserRepository, ids: IdGenerator) uses User.create and users.save, and getUser throws NotFoundError("User", id)

src/application/task-service.ts: private requireProject throws NotFoundError("Project", projectId), a small repeat of ProjectService.getProject's existence check against the same ProjectRepository port
src/application/task-service.ts: private requireUser throws ValidationError for an invalid assignee, which is a different meaning from UserService.getUser's NotFoundError
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All three files are application-layer use-case services with the same shape. Each takes domain ports through its constructor (repositories, IdGenerator, Clock), builds aggregates through the domain factories (Project.create, Task.create, User.create), saves them through the repository ports, and reports missing entities with the domain NotFoundError. Together they cover one concern: orchestrating use cases for the project/task/user domain. None of them touches persistence or the clock directly, so the module's abstractions are not bypassed. Business invariants stay in the domain: task.assignTo and task.markDone own the state changes, and the services do not repeat them. There is some small overlap. TaskService.requireProject repeats the 'project must exist → NotFoundError("Project", id)' check that ProjectService.getProject also does, and TaskService.requireUser looks users up on its own. Both are short lookups against the shared repository port, and requireUser has a different meaning (it throws ValidationError for an invalid assignee). So this is acceptable orchestration, not a duplicated invariant that ought to live in one place.
